label: Problem set 1
title: Problem set 1: Overview of electrode processes
summary: Quantitative practice on the basic vocabulary of the electrode: limiting currents, cell resistance, the RC time constant, capacitive currents, and half-wave potentials.

intro.text: These problems use the working relations of Chapter 1: the steady-state limiting current i = nFAmC, the solution resistance R = l/(kappa A), the RC time constant tau = R C_d, the capacitive current i_c = C_d (dE/dt), and the half-wave potential of a reversible couple.
Each problem is self-contained, and the values are chosen so the arithmetic is clean. Work in mol/cm3 for concentration when the area is in cm2, remembering that 1 M = 1e-3 mol/cm3.

blocks.text: These problems use the working relations of Chapter 1: the steady-state limiting current i = nFAmC, the solution resistance R = l/(kappa A), the RC time constant tau = R C_d, the capacitive current i_c = C_d (dE/dt), and the half-wave potential of a reversible couple.

blocks.title: Limiting current at an RDE
steps: Write the steady-state mass-transfer law: i = nFAmC.
Substitute nF = 96485 C/mol, A = 0.30 cm2, m = 0.010 cm/s, C = 1.0e-5 mol/cm3.

questions.question: A rotating disk electrode of area 0.30 cm2 reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+ from a solution where the mass-transfer coefficient is m = 0.010 cm/s and the concentration is 1.0e-5 mol/cm3. Using i = nFAmC with n = 1 and F = 96485 C/mol, calculate the limiting current in mA.
A 0.10 cm2 planar electrode sits 3.0 cm from a large counter electrode in a solution of conductivity 0.013 ohm-1 cm-1. Calculate the solution resistance between them in ohms, using R = l/(kappa A).
An electrode of area 0.10 cm2 has a double-layer capacitance of 20 uF/cm2, so its total capacitance is 2.0 uF. If the uncompensated resistance is 10 ohm, what is the RC time constant in microseconds?
For the cell above (tau = 20 us), how long in microseconds is needed for double-layer charging to be 95 percent complete? (Use t = 3.0 tau.)
questions.explanation: t = 3.0 x 20 = 60 us. Charging is essentially complete after about three time constants.

questions.question: A 2.0 uF electrode is swept linearly at 1.0 V/s. Neglecting transients, what non-faradaic (capacitive) current flows, in microamperes? (i_c = C dE/dt.)
questions.explanation: i_c = C (dE/dt) = 2.0e-6 x 1.0 = 2.0e-6 A = 2.0 uA. The capacitive current grows with scan rate.

questions.question: At a rotating disk electrode, the limiting current is reached when:
options: Mass transfer supplies the reactant as fast as it can react
questions.explanation: At the limiting current the surface concentration falls to zero and the rate is set entirely by mass transfer, so i = nFAmC.

questions.question: A mercury electrode of area 1.0 cm2 has a double-layer capacitance of 20 uF/cm2. How much charge, in nanocoulombs, is needed to change its potential by 1 mV? (Q = C dE.)
questions.explanation: Q = 20e-6 F x 1e-3 V = 2.0e-8 C = 20 nC. Only a tiny charge moves the potential by 1 mV.

questions.question: The best way to reduce the uncompensated-resistance iR drop between working and reference electrodes is to:
options: Place the reference tip (Luggin capillary) close to the working electrode
questions.explanation: Bringing the reference tip close shortens the path through solution, so R_u and the iR drop both fall.

questions.question: With no current flowing, the interior of a conducting phase is an equipotential volume.
questions.explanation: If an internal field existed, the mobile carriers would move to cancel it. With no current the field is zero and the potential is uniform.

questions.question: A nernstian (electrochemically reversible) half-reaction follows the Nernst equation.
questions.explanation: Nernstian means the potential is linked to concentration by the Nernst equation; it is the fast-electron-transfer limit.

questions.question: Which of the following are real mechanisms for charging an electrode phase? Select all that apply.
options: Pumping electrons in or out with a power supply
Chemical equilibration with a redox couple in solution
Heating the cell to red heat
questions.explanation: Pumping electrons with a power supply and equilibrating chemically with a redox couple are the two mechanisms discussed. Heating is not a charging mechanism.

questions.question: For a reversible system the log plot has a slope of 2.303RT/(nF), equal to 0.05916/n volts per decade at 25 C. What is the slope, in volts per decade, for n = 2?
questions.explanation: Slope = 0.05916/2 = 0.02958 V per decade, about 0.0296 V.

questions.question: For a reversible soluble/soluble couple, the half-wave potential E1/2 is close to:
options: The formal potential E0-prime of the couple
The potential of the reference electrode
The standard potential of the counter electrode
questions.explanation: When oxidized and reduced forms diffuse similarly, E1/2 is close to the formal potential E0-prime.

questions.question: A current of 2.9 mA flows for 20 s. Calculate the charge passed in mC.
A limiting current of 2.9 mA is measured on an electrode of area 0.30 cm2. Calculate the current density in mA/cm2.
A good counter electrode in a three-electrode cell should be:
options: Large, inert and able to pass the required current
questions.explanation: The counter electrode must pass whatever current the working electrode draws without limiting the cell, so it is made large and inert.

questions.question: The capacitive (non-faradaic) current is proportional to the scan rate.
questions.explanation: Because i_c = C (dE/dt), a faster scan drives more charging current, which is why capacitive current is a problem at high scan rates.

questions.question: Which techniques measure the cell current directly? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Chronoamperometry, cyclic voltammetry and polarography all record current. Potentiometry measures potential while drawing essentially no current.
